title: Green Tea Steeping Time & Temperature (Without the Bitterness)
h1: How long to steep green tea
meta_description: Japanese tea guidance steeps green tea about 1 minute at 165–185 °F (74–85 °C); Western guidance says 3–4. Times by type, plus a steep calculator.
keywords: how long to steep green tea
body_html:
Steep green tea at 165–185 °F (74–85 °C), using about 1 teaspoon (2 g) of leaf per 8 oz cup. Japanese tea guidance calls for a brief steep of about 1 minute; general Western guidance suggests 3–4 minutes. Hotter water or a longer steep pulls out more bitterness.

Use the tool above to switch between tea type and see the matching temperature, time, and leaf:water ratio update — the tables below give the same figures for reference if JavaScript is off.

Two conventions for green tea, and why they differ

The Tea Association of the USA's general brewing guidance calls for water at 165–185°F, steeped for approximately one minute, using one teaspoon or one tea bag per cup. Ippodo Tea, a Kyoto tea house whose recipes specify exact temperatures and seconds, lands on the same short-steep convention for its standard sencha: 176°F (80°C) for 60 seconds. Healthline's more general Western guidance runs a degree cooler (175°F / 79°C) but steeps three to four times longer — 3–4 minutes.

Neither figure is wrong; they reflect different traditions. Japanese sencha service treats green tea as a fast-extracting leaf meant for a short steep poured in small rounds, often re-infused. The more general Western convention treats a cup of tea as a single, longer infusion meant to fully extract in one pour. Start with the short steep for a lighter, sweeter cup — lengthen it toward 3–4 minutes only if you prefer a stronger, more traditionally Western cup and don't mind more astringency.

Healthline's own steeping guidance singles green tea out for this reason: "green tea is the most delicate, while black and herbal teas are more forgiving when it comes to temperature and steeping time." A black tea or herbal tisane brewed a minute long or a few degrees hot barely changes; green tea brewed the same way over-extracts fast, which is exactly why its published times sit so much shorter than black tea's 3–5 minutes at a near-boil.

Note the leaf:water ratios aren't identical either: Ippodo's standard sencha brew is more concentrated, meant for small cups poured across a session, while the Tea Association's one-teaspoon-per-8-oz-cup guideline matches the single large Western mug. That's a serving-style difference, not a disagreement about temperature.

No thermometer? Here's the low-tech version

The Tea Association of the USA's own instructions don't assume you own a thermometer: bring water to a full boil, take it off the heat, and let it sit for ten minutes before pouring it over the leaf. That resting time is what gets a rolling 212°F boil down into the 165–185°F green tea range without any measuring. It's a slower version of the same trick used for Ippodo's 176°F sencha standard — boil, then let the kettle cool for a few minutes before pouring — just calibrated for a wider target range.

Steep time by green tea type

"Green tea" isn't one leaf. Even within Ippodo's own Japanese convention, sencha, gyokuro, and genmaicha steep at different temperatures and times because they're different leaf styles:

TypeLeafWaterWater tempSteep time
Sencha10 g (2 tbsp)7 oz (210 ml)176°F (80°C)60 sec
Gyokuro10 g (2 tbsp)3 oz (80 ml)140°F (60°C)90 sec
Genmaicha10 g (2 tbsp)8 oz (240 ml)212°F (100°C)30 sec

Gyokuro, a shade-grown leaf prized for a sweeter, less astringent cup, steeps cooler and longer in far less water than sencha — a small, concentrated pour rather than a full mug. That lower temperature is deliberate: gyokuro's shade-growing process makes for a more delicate leaf than sun-grown sencha, so Ippodo's own recipe drops the water 36°F cooler (140°F vs. 176°F) to avoid scorching it, even though the steep runs half a minute longer to compensate. Genmaicha, green tea blended with roasted rice, is the opposite case: Ippodo's own recipe calls for full-boiling water, but for just 30 seconds, since the roasted rice component extracts quickly and turns bitter or scorched-tasting if left in longer. There's no single "green tea" number that fits all three; steep by type, not by a single rule of thumb.

Multiple infusions

Good sencha and gyokuro leaves aren't single-use. Ippodo's own sharing method for sencha and gyokuro repeats the same steep-and-pour cycle — after the first measured steep, later pours use no added wait time, filling a pitcher round after round rather than stopping at a fixed count of two or three steeps. Healthline notes that loose-leaf tea can be re-infused, and cites research finding that most loose-leaf teas still showed measurable antioxidant activity after a sixth brew — a description of what that research measured, not a promise about any single cup. There's no one "correct" number of re-steeps; leaf quality and how long the previous steep ran both matter more than a fixed count. A quick first steep, like sencha's 60 seconds, tends to leave more flavor in the leaf for a strong second pour than a long first steep that's already extracted most of it.

Does a longer steep add caffeine?

Yes. Healthline's steeping guidance states that steeping tea for an extra minute increases caffeine content by up to 29%, and that brewing with boiling-temperature water increases it by up to 66%. That's one reason a quick, cooler Japanese-style steep and a longer, hotter Western-style steep don't land at the same caffeine level even from the same leaf. See our green tea caffeine breakdown for the full range and how it compares to coffee, black tea, and matcha.

Putting it together

Short version: for a fast, lighter cup, use the Japanese convention — 165–185°F for about 1 minute, or 176°F for exactly 60 seconds if you're following Ippodo's sencha standard. For a stronger, more traditional Western cup, Healthline's general guidance is 175°F for 3–4 minutes; expect more bitterness and a bit more caffeine at that end. Adjust further by leaf type rather than using one number for every green tea: gyokuro wants 140°F for about 90 seconds, and genmaicha wants a full boil but only 30 seconds. None of these figures are interchangeable, and that's the point — matching the steep to the leaf, not to a single memorized rule, is what keeps green tea from turning bitter.

For general green tea troubleshooting beyond steep time and temperature, see our how to brew green tea guide. For how green tea's temperature compares with black, oolong, white, and matcha side by side, see our tea brewing temperature guide. For matcha, which is whisked whole rather than steeped and strained, see matcha to water ratio.

This describes published preparation guidance and general information, not medical or dietary advice.

sources.title: How to Steep Tea Like an Expert

faqs.q: How long should you steep green tea?
faqs.a: About 165–185°F for roughly 1 minute is the short, Japanese sencha convention — the Tea Association of the USA and Ippodo Tea's standard sencha recipe (176°F for 60 seconds) both land here. General Western guidance from Healthline suggests a longer, cooler steep: 175°F for 3–4 minutes. Both are published; try the short steep first for a lighter, sweeter cup.

faqs.q: What temperature should you use for green tea?
faqs.a: 165–185°F (74–85°C), per the Tea Association of the USA's general brewing guidance. Ippodo Tea's standard sencha recipe specifies 176°F (80°C) exactly; Healthline's general guidance is close, at 175°F (79°C). Avoid a full, rolling boil — it scorches green tea's delicate leaf.

Yes. Healthline's steeping guidance found that a hotter temperature or longer steep isn't necessarily better for green tea — in studies, tea brewed that way scored lower for color, flavor, and aroma. Steeping for an extra minute also increases caffeine content by up to 29%, and boiling water by up to 66%, per the same source.

faqs.q: How many times can you steep green tea?
faqs.a: There's no fixed number. Ippodo Tea's own method for sencha and gyokuro repeats the same steep-and-pour cycle with no added wait time between rounds, rather than stopping at two or three steeps. Healthline notes loose-leaf tea can be re-infused, and cites research finding many loose-leaf teas still showed antioxidant activity after a sixth brew.

faqs.q: Why is my green tea bitter?
faqs.a: Almost always water that's too hot or a steep that ran too long. Green tea's short 165–185°F, roughly 1-minute Japanese convention is deliberately brief for this reason; if you're using the longer 3–4 minute Western guidance and it tastes harsh, try dropping the temperature or shortening the steep first.

product_bridge_blurb: Timing a steep to the second isn't for everyone. Spice Rush is a caffeinated black-tea blend that's forgiving if you let it sit a little longer.
